blocks.content: A caldera is a large, basin-shaped depression formed when the summit of a volcano collapses into its emptied magma chamber.

rows: Formed by explosive ejection of material around the vent
Formed by structural collapse into an emptied magma chamber
Relatively small, usually less than 1-2 km in diameter
Massive basin, often 10 to 50+ km in diameter
Funnel-shaped or bowl-shaped opening at the summit
Broad, flat-bottomed depression often filled with a lake

items: Magma vs. Lava: Molten rock is called magma while subterranean, but becomes lava once it erupts onto the surface.
Crater vs. Caldera: Craters are formed by explosive ejection around vents, whereas calderas are much larger structures formed by downward structural collapse.
Parasitic Features: Questions often ask about side vents and parasitic cones formed along lateral fissures on volcanic flanks.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The magma chamber is a large pool of molten rock located beneath the surface of the Earth.
The main vent is the pipe or central channel through which magma travels upward toward the surface.
A crater is a funnel-shaped depression at the top of a volcano surrounding the main vent.
A caldera is formed when the summit of a volcano collapses into an emptied magma chamber following a major eruption.
Secondary or parasitic cones develop on the flanks of a volcano when magma escapes through lateral cracks.
